title: Tehran is a Different Beast Now
gist: Former CIA analyst Cole Bucy argues decapitation strikes created a harder-line 'New Tehran' that cannot be deterred, sees time on its side via the Strait of Hormuz and energy-price pain, and may pursue nuclear weapons; he urges the US to cut losses with a creative ceasefire.

insights.claim: The US-Israeli decapitation strikes, including the killing of Ali Khamenei on the war's first day in February, shifted Iran's center of gravity toward military hardliners around Mojtaba Khamenei, who lack Ali Khamenei's caution.
insights.speaker: Cole Bucy
insights.so_what: Don't assume internal splits will produce a softer Iran; hardline posture is likely to persist.
insights.locator: The Tehran that the world knew is gone

insights.claim: Surviving Iranian leaders likely see themselves as 'dead men walking' who expect further decapitation strikes, which erodes US and Israeli deterrence though they are not suicidal.
insights.speaker: Cole Bucy
insights.so_what: Deterrence by threat is weaker, raising escalation risk including around the US midterms.

insights.claim: Iran views Israel's threat as endemic but the US threat as existential, and reads Trump's threats as unlikely to exceed what Iran has already endured.
insights.speaker: Cole Bucy
insights.so_what: Escalation threats have diminishing marginal effect on Tehran.

insights.claim: Hardliners probably concluded that Ali Khamenei's acceptance of ceasefires in 2019 and after the 12-day war last summer ultimately cost him his life.
insights.speaker: Cole Bucy
insights.so_what: Raises odds Tehran rejects off-ramps that look like weakness.

insights.claim: The US-Israeli attack flipped Iran's calculus on closing the Strait of Hormuz; because the US struck without consulting allies, Europe and Asia will not join a coalition to reopen it.
insights.speaker: Cole Bucy
insights.so_what: A coalition-backed reopening is unlikely, extending shipping and energy disruption.

insights.claim: US operations since August (escorts, mine clearing, striking launch sites) briefly almost restored prewar shipping levels in late September, but Iranian tanker attacks in early October reached the highest levels of the war, pushing down traffic and raising per-tanker costs.
insights.speaker: Cole Bucy
insights.so_what: Hormuz transit remains fragile; per-tanker costs and insurance stay elevated.
insights.locator: The U.S. military has performed impressive work

insights.claim: The strait's partial closure has hurt exports of LNG, fertilizers and especially diesel, while Houthi control of Bab al-Mandeb coast and repeated damage to Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline add stress; Tehran expects oil prices to climb enough to buckle US resolve.
insights.speaker: Cole Bucy
insights.so_what: Energy tail risk skews upward: diesel, LNG and fertilizer shortages are cited alongside crude.
insights.locator: New Tehran is skeptical that the U.S. economy

insights.claim: Iran warns it would hit Gulf Arab civilian infrastructure if the US bombs Iranian water and electricity, and Gulf states privately plead with Trump to avoid that escalation.
insights.speaker: Cole Bucy
insights.so_what: Gulf infrastructure is a vulnerable escalation target.
insights.locator: A red line Trump has threatened

insights.claim: Iran believes it can outlast US resolve: it has a survivalist economy, cites the Iran-Iraq war as grit, and sees economic hardship as not linearly causing revolt, as in North Korea and Venezuela.
insights.speaker: Cole Bucy
insights.so_what: Don't price a near-term regime collapse from the blockade.
insights.locator: Confident It Can Outlast American Resolve

insights.claim: Russia and China reportedly supplied Iran with missile and drone components, munitions and potential targeting intelligence, and Iran counts on Beijing honoring its deposits in Chinese banks.
insights.speaker: Cole Bucy
insights.so_what: Great-power backing lengthens Iran's staying power.
insights.locator: New Tehran almost certainly is counting

insights.claim: Iran sees the US abandoning regional bases and running low on missiles and interceptors, and hopes to turn Gulf states against hosting US forces.
insights.speaker: Cole Bucy
insights.so_what: Interceptor stock depletion is an emerging US constraint.

insights.claim: Iran's deal red lines have stayed unchanged although Hormuz leverage eroded for two months, which suggests a fixed bar tied to the June Memorandum of Understanding's gains, including Iranian control of the strait jointly with Oman and sanctions relief without nuclear concessions.
insights.speaker: Cole Bucy
insights.so_what: A deal needs durable US concessions; a limited ceasefire looks unlikely.

insights.claim: Bucy predicts a surviving regime will rebuild its missile and drone programs, regrow proxies, and may reconsider nuclear weapons, possibly soon.
insights.speaker: Cole Bucy
insights.so_what: Nuclear breakout risk rises if the regime survives.

insights.claim: The clearest sign that old instincts are returning would be Iran accepting a simple blockade-for-blockade ceasefire that ends the double enclosure of the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Cole Bucy
insights.so_what: A concrete signpost for de-escalation and oil relief.
insights.locator: The clearest sign that Iranian leaders

insights.claim: Bucy advises the US to recognize the war as a misstep and cut losses with creative arrangements such as a multilateral ceasefire forum, congressional war-powers and sanctions actions, and a rollback in regional basing.
insights.speaker: Cole Bucy
insights.so_what: Policy direction he advocates; the White House faces political costs.
insights.locator: While there are no easy solutions
